text: A note, rolled up inside a finger. "Dining car, nine o'clock. Vasko never looks at waiters. I."
And in the thumb, a lady's nail file. Thin, steel and very useful.
Mountains, moonlight and a very long way down. The Iron Arrow is climbing towards the Zlatá pass.
Bogdan's tea, still steaming. Karvonian railways run on tea and arguments.
Two glasses of tea, stone cold. Nobody has offered me a fresh one. I'm a prisoner, not a passenger.
Karvonian handcuffs, heavy and cold, chained to the luggage rail. Kolar has a future in furniture removals.
I pull. The luggage rail doesn't. It was built to carry pianos.
Click. One nail file, one lock, thirty seconds. Technical Section would be proud. Ilse would be prouder.
Ilse dropped a glove at my feet on her way out. Ladies don't drop gloves by accident. Not that lady.
Just out of reach of my hands. Not out of reach of a size ten shoe.
There's something inside it. I should take a closer look.
Springs, and a very old sandwich. Ilse wasn't lying about the sandwich.
The berth where I hid the plans. Ilse lifted this mattress and told Vasko there was nothing under it.
I can't reach it from here. The chain's a foot too short.
Just the sandwich now. I'll leave that for Kolar.
Still here. Forty sheets of Nightglass. She saw them, and she said nothing.
A brass bell push. "Conductor." In Karvonia, even calling for help comes with a form.
It's by the door, and I'm chained to the rack. Out of reach.
Bogdan is busy arguing with Kolar. I shouldn't interrupt a Karvonian argument. They go on for years.
I'd love to. But I'm chained to the furniture.
Quiet in there, Harrow! Or I come in and make you quiet.
Not without the plans. They're under that mattress.
Search him, Captain.
A passport for Herr Harwig, refrigerators. A hairpin. And a photograph.
Anička. Your daughter looks well, Ilse. She is travelling with my sister, in first class. Such a treat for her.
Yes, Colonel.
Search the compartment, Ilse. Mr Harrow was carrying forty sheets of my property.
Nothing, Colonel. Only springs, and a very old sandwich.
She saw them. She saw them, and she lied to his face.
Then he threw them into the snow. No matter. In Moscow, Mr Harrow will tell us everything, slowly.
Stay, Englishman. Like a good dog.
Dinner is at nine, in the dining car. You, sadly, are not invited.
Goodbye, Jack. Enjoy Moscow.
I am right outside, Harrow. I do not sleep, and I do not like you.
Coming, coming!
You rang, comrade? Tea, blankets, a glass of kefir? And tickets, please.
My ticket is with the gentleman outside. Captain Kolar has all my papers.
Captain! This passenger's ticket, please. And yours.
Mine? I am military. I travel free.
Nobody travels free on my carriage, Captain. Not the Marshal, not the Pope, and certainly not you.
This is an outrage! We will see the Colonel about this!
We will! And the Colonel will buy a ticket too!
Karvonian bureaucracy. The only force on earth more stubborn than the Karvonian army.
The dining car is forward, the mail van is behind. And for once, nobody is pointing anything at me.
Compartment one. Somebody inside is snoring like a sawmill in a thunderstorm.
The snoring stops. Then starts again, louder. That's a no.
Compartment three. A sign says "Do not disturb. Delegation of the Karvonian Tractor Institute."
Someone shouts something about tractors. I don't think it's an invitation.
The linen cupboard. Sheets, blankets, and whatever else the Iron Arrow keeps folded.
Sheets and blankets. My own coat is folded on the top shelf, next to a very surprised pillow.
Sheets, blankets... and a spare waiter's jacket, with a bow tie clipped to the lapel.
A waiter's jacket. Might come in handy, if I knew what I was walking into.
Vasko never looks at waiters, Ilse says. Tonight, he's going to be served by one.
White jacket, black bow tie. Nobody ever looks twice at a waiter. Nobody ever looks once.
The emergency brake. "Misuse will be punished with a fine of five hundred roubles." And, I suspect, the Colonel.
Stop the train here, in the middle of nowhere, with Vasko on board? Not yet. Hold that thought.
A fire axe behind glass. "In case of fire." Or conductors.
Bogdan's cabin: a samovar, a timetable and a certificate. "Conductor of the Year, 1979, 1980, 1981 and 1983." One wonders what happened in 1982.
Karvograd twenty three fifty nine, the Zlatá pass at two ten, the border at four forty. Then Moscow, and a very long conversation with Vasko.
Vasko is somewhere up there. I shouldn't go charging in without a plan.
Vasko is in the dining car. I can't stroll in wearing my own face. Ilse said he never looks at waiters...
Waiter. Why are there geese following you?
Chef's special, Colonel.
Excellent. Carry on.
Vasko, Ilse, Kolar and the conductor. And the waiter is me. Let's hope Ilse knows her Colonel.
Waiter! Champagne. And not the Dom Pérignon, I am sick of Dom Pérignon.
Moonlight on the snow, and pine forests rushing past. The Iron Arrow is climbing the Zlatá pass.
Tonight: borscht, borscht, or borscht. I'll have the borscht.
The galley: steam, copper pans and a cook in a very tall hat.
The chef has a moustache like a boot brush and a hat like a wedding cake. I know that moustache.
Colonel Vasko at dinner, with a napkin under his chin and his medals dangerously close to the borscht.
More champagne, waiter. It is revolting. I cannot stop.
Champagne, waiter! Why are you standing there like a lamp post?
Bread? I ordered champagne, you idiot!
Show the Colonel his own blueprints? Even Vasko would look at the waiter then.
Ilse, in black, with a glove missing. She hasn't looked at me once. She's very good.
Not now, waiter. The Colonel is waiting for his champagne.
Go, Jack. First class. And remember: the Danube looks blue tonight.
Kolar, still arguing about his ticket. He hasn't looked at the waiter either. Waiters are invisible in Karvonia.
Not now, waiter! I am explaining military law to a man in a hat.
Bogdan, Conductor of the Year, refusing to lose an argument in front of the Colonel.
Tickets, please! Oh, you are staff. Carry on, comrade.
First class is forward. I should talk to Ilse before I go wandering.
Franz?
Shh! On this train I am Chef Frantisek. The real chef had a small accident with a bottle of slivovitz.
What sort of accident?
I gave it to him. He is asleep in the coal tender, very happy.
London sent me after you, Herr Harrow. Also, nobody else on this train can make a borscht.
What does the waiter need?
Champagne for the Colonel. Not the Dom Pérignon.
Soviet champagne, semi-sweet. Very semi, very sweet. He will hate it, and drink the whole bottle.
Have you got any bread? It's for some geese.
Of course it is. Bread from Tuesday, hard enough to stop a bullet. Geese will follow it to the end of the earth.
How is the borscht?
Red, hot and angry, like the Colonel. But the borscht has more taste.
Back to work.
Mind the soup, Herr Harrow.
More, waiter. More.
Hm. You look familiar, waiter.
All waiters look alike, Colonel.
True. I never look at them.
Sweet. Revolting. Pour me another.
Waiter, a glass of water, please.
Your water, madame.
You found my glove.
And the nail file. Why, Ilse?
Because my daughter is on this train, Jack. In first class, with Vasko's sister Olga. He brings Anička everywhere, so that I remember who I belong to.
Then we take her back.
The mail van is the last car. Uncouple it at the top of the pass, and it will roll all the way down to Zlatá Hora.
And Olga?
Olga never lets the child out of her sight. She is afraid of nothing in this world, except birds.
Birds?
She once fainted because of a pigeon. Tell Anička the Danube looks blue tonight, and she will go with you.
Only when it rains.
Go. I will meet you in the mail van.
Birds. And I know exactly where to find three very angry geese.
Velvet, brass, another portrait of Vasko, and a lady who looks like she could bend railway lines with her knitting needles.
A waiter? I ordered nothing. Go away.
Another Vasko. He's everywhere on this train, like damp.
The pass is close now. Snow, rock, and a very long way down.
A game of chess, half played. White is losing badly. White was brave enough to play Olga.
A thick Turkish carpet. You could lose a goose in it. Several, in fact.
Locked. "Nobody drives the Iron Arrow but the driver and God," says the sign. God has the night off.
Olga Vasko, the Colonel's sister. Spectacles on a chain, knitting needles like bayonets, and the warmth of a Siberian bus stop.
Tea for the young lady, madame?
The child takes no tea after eight o'clock. Children who drink tea after eight grow up to be poets.
Heaven forbid.
Exactly. Go away.
Crumbs? On my carpet? Are you mad?
Show Vasko's sister the blueprints? I'd rather show them to the geese.
A little girl in a blue coat, with plaits and a rag doll, pressing her nose to the window. She has her mother's eyes, and her mother's look of someone planning an escape.
Aunt Olga says I must not talk to waiters.
Anička! Away from the waiter, he is probably a poet.
Olga won't let her out of her sight. Not unless something truly terrible happens. Something with feathers.
Oops. Tuesday's bread, all over the carpet. Clumsy of me.
BIRDS! Birds on my carpet! Get them away from me!
Geese! Aunt Olga, there are geese on the train!
Anička. Your mama says the Danube looks blue tonight.
Only when it rains! Mama taught me that!
Then come with me, quickly. Your mama is waiting.
Guards! Geese! GUARDS!
Anička! My darling, my brave girl.
Mama! A waiter brought me! And there are geese everywhere!
Thank you, Jack. Whatever happens now, thank you.
Thank me at the bottom of the mountain. Hold on to something.
The mail van, and my old friends the geese. Somebody has fed them. It wasn't Kolar.
Vasko on his horse, with a hole in his back where the plans used to be. Karvonian art has never looked better.
Three geese in a slatted crate. They look at me like I owe them money.
Honk. Not without a very good reason to follow me, apparently.
A crumb of Tuesday's bread, and suddenly I'm the most popular man in Karvonia. Come along, ladies. First class awaits.
My old crowbar, where I dropped it on the way up to the roof.
We've been through a lot together, you and I.
Sacks of letters to Moscow. Some of them will arrive a lot sooner than others.
Through the gangway door: the coupling to the sleeping car. One pin between us and a very long ride downhill.
Not yet. Anička is still up in first class with her aunt.
The coupling pin is frozen solid. I need leverage.
Back up the train, past a carriage full of furious geese and an aunt on an armchair? No, thank you.
Still locked from the outside. Kolar is nothing if not consistent.
The pin's out!
The train is going on without us.
Why is it so quiet?
Jack... we are rolling backwards.
Downhill, all the way to Zlatá Hora. Somebody find the brake.
Never mind. I've found it.
Zlatá Hora. Altitude one thousand four hundred metres. Population three.
The Colonel. She rode the roof all the way down the mountain and she wants a medal for it.
The mail van, at rest at last. It will need a very long letter of apology.
Zlatá Hora. Altitude one thousand four hundred metres, population three. Plus one spy, one ex-spy, and a very small girl.
Forty sheets of Nightglass. Real, this time. I checked twice. Then a third time, for luck.
Mama, can we keep one of the geese?
No, darling. The geese are going to Moscow. They have a very important meeting with Aunt Olga.
Mama! One of them came with us! On the roof!
She rode all the way down. Five bends, one tunnel, and not a feather out of place.
Then she is braver than the Karvonian army. Very well, Anička. She can stay.
I will call her Colonel.
Good morning, darlings!
Madame Novak?
Control sends his regards. He also wants to know why you have stolen a mail van.
You work for London?
Darling, I am Control's mother. Who do you think got him the job?
And the chocolates on the train?
Expenses, darling. They were delicious.
You knew about me. All along.
I know about everybody, darling. It is a mother's job.
Mama, what was that?
That, darling, is the other problem.
That was Nightglass. But the plans are right here, in my pocket.
Vasko did not steal the plans to build it, Jack. He stole them because he had already built it.
Ilse dropped her glove at my feet. On purpose, I'd bet my pension on it.
There's something inside that glove. I should take a closer look at it.
A nail file and a pair of handcuffs. Every schoolboy's dream.
The plans are still under the mattress, where Ilse left them.
Kolar is outside that door. I need someone to take him away. Someone with a whistle and a grudge.
The door is open. The dining car is forward.
Vasko never looks at waiters. That linen cupboard might have a uniform.
Ilse's glove might tell me what she has in mind.
The dining car is forward. Ilse will be there at nine.
Geese, for Aunt Olga. They're in the mail van at the back of the train.
Lead the ladies forward, through the dining car to first class.
The Colonel is waiting for his champagne.
Vasko wants champagne. The chef will have some, and I know the chef.
Ilse asked the waiter for water. I should see what she really wants.
Geese need a reason to follow a man. Franz might have some bread.
Bread in my pocket, geese in the mail van. The mail van is at the back of the train.
First class is forward. The ladies are ready.
Olga is afraid of nothing but birds. There are three geese in the mail van, and they like bread.
A little bread on Olga's carpet, and the geese will do the rest.
The coupling, at the front end of the van. One pin, and we're free.
That coupling pin is frozen. My old crowbar is lying on the floor.
I need to talk to Ilse before anything else. She'll be in the dining car.
Geese need a good reason to follow me. Franz's kitchen will have one.
A little of Tuesday's bread for the geese, and they'll follow me anywhere.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
The brake blocks are on fire! Give them a second!
Jack, how fast are we going?
Again! Again!
Ilse, is that a goose on the roof?
Don't look at her, Jack. It only encourages her.
I think I left my stomach at the last bend.
Faster, Mister Jack!
Not faster! Slower! Slower is the good one!
About sixty. Backwards.
Jack Harrow stole Colonel Vasko's portrait, and the Nightglass plans hidden inside it, and fought his way along the roof of the Iron Arrow.
He hid the plans under a mattress. Then the door opened, and there stood Vasko, Kolar, and Ilse.
It is already flying.
Aunt Olga has been standing on an armchair for four hours. The geese have not moved.
Chapter Four: Nightglass.
A black kid glove, still warm, that Ilse dropped at my feet. Ladies don't drop gloves by accident. Not this lady.
A lady's steel nail file, hidden in the glove. Thin enough for a keyhole. Ilse, you're a genius.
Forty sheets of blueprint, rolled tight and stamped NIGHTGLASS. Slightly flatter for a night under a mattress.
Sovetskoye Shampanskoye, semi-sweet. Very semi, very sweet. The Colonel will hate it.
Bread from Tuesday. Hard enough to stop a bullet. Franz says geese will follow it anywhere.
The railway crowbar from the mail van. We've been through a lot together.
